Major Jonathan Ladd (September 26, 1819 – April 9, 1889) was an American lawyer, civil administrator, and Union Army paymaster during the American Civil War. He served as Union Master of Transportation for Massachusetts volunteers and later as Additional Paymaster for the U.S. Volunteers. Ladd was listed in Brigadier General Henry L. Burnett’s report among those present at the deathbed of Abraham Lincoln, and his presentation watch—saved from melting at a Lowell scrap yard in the 1970s—sparked renewed interest in his life and career.
Early life and legal career
Jonathan Ladd was born in Alexandria, New Hampshire, on September 26, 1819, to **Josiah Ladd (1792–1864)** and **Eliza (Crawford) Ladd (1794–1871)**. In 1833 his family moved to Lowell, Massachusetts, where he became a farmer, attorney, alderman, justice of the peace, and local politician. He descended from **Daniel Ladd (1613–1693)** of Haverhill, Massachusetts, a colonial settler whose line produced Revolutionary War veterans.
Union Master of Transportation and the Baltimore Riot (1861)
When President Abraham Lincoln called for volunteers after the attack on Fort Sumter, Governor John Albion Andrew appointed Ladd as **Master of Transportation** for Massachusetts volunteers. Working from the **Fifth Avenue Hotel** in New York City, he organized rail and steamship transport for the 5th, 6th, and 8th Massachusetts Regiments to Washington within 48 hours of Lincoln’s proclamation.
On **April 19, 1861**, the Baltimore Riot of 1861 resulted in the first Union casualties of the war, including Ladd’s 17‑year‑old cousin **Luther C. Ladd**. His dying words “All Hail to the Stars and Stripes” appeared on patriotic envelopes issued by the War Department to bolster Union morale.
Ladd’s telegrams to General Benjamin F. Butler and Governor Andrew relayed the riot and casualties. When rail service was cut off, he chartered the steamships *Ariel* and *De Soto* “on his own responsibility and in the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts” to carry 1,200 men of the 5th Massachusetts to Washington, a decision praised in the *New York Tribune* of 22 April 1861.
His initiative ensured reinforcements for Washington and earned him federal recognition.
Promotion to Major and Paymaster Department Service (1861–1864)
On **June 1, 1861**, Ladd was promoted to **Major and Additional Paymaster U.S. Volunteers**, confirmed by the Senate and listed in the *New York Times* of August 7, 1861. Stationed in Washington D.C., he supervised military payrolls and finance operations and was closely associated with the Paymaster’s Department, the War Department, and the Treasury. He maintained ties to family members Hannibal Hamlin and Lafayette Sabine Foster.
Gold Presentation Watch (1864)
In March 1864 the officers of the 2nd Connecticut Volunteer Artillery Regiment presented Ladd with a solid‑gold “Appleton Tracy grade” watch (serial no. 50,141) made by the American Watch Company (Waltham, Massachusetts). The 18‑karat Robbins & Appleton case contained 15 jewels and a gold balance. The engraving read “Presented to Major Jonathan Ladd by the Officers of the 2d Connecticut Volunteer Artillery, March 1864.”
Colonel **Elisha Strong Kellogg**, who made the presentation, was killed three months later at the Battle of Cold Harbor. The regiment lost 323 men in its first major action, and Ladd was responsible for the financial records afterward.
Mosby’s Greenback Raid (1864)
On **October 14, 1864**, while at the United States Hotel in Martinsburg, Virginia, Ladd witnessed the aftermath of Colonel John S. Mosby’s Greenback Raid, a Confederate attack on a Baltimore and Ohio Railroad train carrying payroll funds. He telegraphed Paymaster General **Benjamin W. Brice** that the train was burned and Paymasters **David Ruggles** and **Edwin Moore** were taken prisoner. Among those guarding Ladd and the government funds was **Brigadier General William Henry Seward Jr.**, son of Secretary William H. Seward. Ruggles later died in Confederate captivity; Moore was released.
Lincoln’s Deathbed (1865)
A report by **Brigadier General Henry L. Burnett**, Judge Advocate for the Lincoln assassination investigation, lists “Generals Halleck, Meigs, Farnsworth, Augur, and Ladd” among those present at 7:22 a.m. on April 15, 1865, when Lincoln died. The document is held at the **Goshen Historical Society** (Goshen, New York). The Ladd Archive identifies the “General Ladd” as Major Jonathan Ladd, then Paymaster in Washington.
Investigation and Disciplinary Proceedings
In late 1864 the War Department investigated Ladd for selling pocket watches to enlisted men at a profit. The Judge Advocate General’s Office found no embezzlement but issued a formal reprimand. The incident ended his prospects for promotion but did not erase his standing as an able officer.
Return to Lowell and Efforts to Clear His Record (1865–1869)
After dismissal in 1865, Ladd returned to Lowell and became President of the **Middlesex North Agricultural Society**, purchasing a farm in Tewksbury. He remained active as a lawyer and member of the Lowell Bar Association. He hired Boston attorney **Richard S. Spofford** to petition for revision of his service status from “dismissed” to “mustered out.” Spofford appealed to President Andrew Johnson, Secretary Edwin M. Stanton, General William Tecumseh Sherman, Assistant Secretary **Thomas Eckert**, and Judge Advocate General **Joseph Holt**, asserting that Ladd was “summarily dismissed to gratify the revenge of Baker,” referring to Union spy Lafayette C. Baker.
Elmira Prison Camp and Ladd’s Appeal to President Johnson
According to the Ladd Archive, he served briefly at the Elmira Prison Camp in New York, possibly to collect intelligence from Confederate prisoners. Baker was instrumental in prosecuting Ladd, though the exact nature of his motives is unknown. Documents show endorsements by Holt, Sherman, Stanton, and President Johnson. Johnson’s notation read: “Let the order dismissing Major Ladd be so modified as to honorably discharge him from the date of dismissal.”
While Ladd had profited from watch sales, historians note that his initiative in April 1861 to charter transports for Massachusetts troops was crucial to defending Washington and may have influenced President Johnson’s clemency decision.
Later Life and Death
Ladd continued to live in Lowell, serving in civic organizations and veterans’ groups. He died on **April 9, 1889**, the anniversary of Robert E. Lee’s surrender, and was buried in Massachusetts.
Rediscovery and Continuing Research
Ladd was largely forgotten until his gold watch was rescued from ALCO Scrap Metal in Lowell during the 1970s by **Robert Betty**, who researched its history using library index cards. Later, collector **Paul Mellen** acquired the watch and expanded the research through the *National Association of Watch and Clock Collectors* and archives in Lowell and Goshen. Their findings linked Ladd to the Baltimore Riot, Mosby’s Greenback Raid, Elmira Prison, and Lincoln’s deathbed, as well as President Johnson’s order changing his record to an honorable discharge.
Legacy
Major Ladd symbolizes the administrative backbone of the Union Army and the ethical dilemmas faced by paymasters serving under fire. His recovered watch connects Civil War history and American horology. Ladd’s life and artifacts are featured in Paul Mellen’s *Who Really Shot Abraham Lincoln* (Patriot Publishing, 2020) and the Fox Nation documentary of the same name hosted by Lenny DePaul.
